title: Ex 8.13 · Removing a union
prompt: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be any sets. Prove that $A - (B \cup C) = (A - B) \cap (A - C)$.
answer_format: A chain of lines, each a set (like A ∪ (B ∩ C)) or a statement about an element x (like x ∈ A or x ∈ B). Each line must have exactly the same elements as the line before; start from the left side and end at the right side.
hints: x ∈ A − (B ∪ C) means x ∈ A and not (x ∈ B or x ∈ C).
De Morgan's law turns not (x ∈ B or x ∈ C) into x ∉ B and x ∉ C.
x ∈ A is the same as (x ∈ A and x ∈ A), so you can regroup into (x ∈ A and x ∉ B) and (x ∈ A and x ∉ C).
solution: Let $x$ be any element. Then $x \in A - (B \cup C)$ means $x \in A \land \sim(x \in B \lor x \in C)$, which by De Morgan's law is $x \in A \land x \notin B \land x \notin C$.
Because $x \in A$ is equivalent to $x \in A \land x \in A$, we can regroup this as $(x \in A \land x \notin B) \land (x \in A \land x \notin C)$.
That says $x \in A - B$ and $x \in A - C$, so $x \in (A - B) \cap (A - C)$.
Every step was an equivalence, so $A - (B \cup C) = (A - B) \cap (A - C)$. $\blacksquare$

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses Section 8.3 (proving A = B), the definitions of union, intersection and difference (Section 1.5) and the logic laws of Section 2.6.

x ∈ A and (x ∉ B and x ∉ C)
(x ∈ A and x ∉ B) and (x ∈ A and x ∉ C)
x ∈ A − B and x ∈ A − C
